paper_a.title: A statistical model for tensor PCA

paper_b.title: Statistical limits of spiked tensor models

metadata.description: Both papers study the spiked tensor model T = lambda x^{otimes d} + W. Richard-Montanari (paper A) introduce the model and analyze it from an algorithmic / statistical-physics angle: ML upper bounds, tensor unfolding, power iteration, AMP with state evolution, PSD-cone-constrained projection, plus a Fano-style information-theoretic lower bound. Perry-Wein-Bandeira (paper B) extend the same model to a sharper statistical-decision-theoretic analysis: they derive matching contiguity-based detection/recovery lower bounds for general priors via a noise-conditioned second-moment method, treat spherical / Rademacher / sparse-Rademacher priors uniformly, and tighten the spherical upper bound below mu_d using a BBP eigenvalue argument. The relationship is best classified as EXT: B inherits A's setup and ABC noise-norm result, then extends to an optimal information-theoretic theory across multiple priors.

matches.explanation: Both define the spiked tensor model: a rank-one symmetric tensor lambda * v^{otimes k/d} (resp. beta * z^{otimes k}) plus symmetric Gaussian noise. The two definitions differ only in normalization of the noise (paper A uses sqrt(k/n), paper B uses Wigner conventions with N(0,2/n) entries) and in whether the spike vector has a fixed law (B uses a prior X, A treats z as deterministic unit vector); these are notational variations of the same object.

Paper A's symmetric standard normal noise tensor and paper B's Wigner tensor WT(d) are the same Gaussian symmetric tensor ensemble up to the n-scaling convention (1/sqrt(n) front factor in A versus 2/n entry variance in B). Both are obtained by symmetrizing an asymmetric i.i.d. Gaussian tensor.

Paper A's tensor operator norm and paper B's injective norm of a tensor are both defined as the maximum of <T, x^{otimes d}> over the unit sphere (paper A states the multilinear version with k unit vectors; for symmetric tensors this is equivalent to the symmetric-rank-one form used by B).

Paper A's tensor-vector product map X{v} is an operational definition used by power iteration and AMP. Paper B does not use iterative algorithms in the order-d tensor space, so this map has no counterpart.
Paper A's sign-symmetric loss Loss(v_hat, v_z) = 2 - 2|<v_hat, v_z>| is paper-A-specific; paper B measures recovery via E[<x, x_hat>^d] >= eps (weak recovery; see DP403.7), not a metric loss.
Unfolding (matricization) operator M_q is central to paper A's tensor-unfolding algorithm but is not used in paper B's purely information-theoretic analysis.

Paper A's spherical p-spin Hamiltonian H_Z(v) = <Z, v^{otimes k}> appears in the appendix to import Auffinger-Ben Arous-Cerny. Paper B uses the same idea implicitly (through TP403.2 and the formula in EP403.3) but never names the Hamiltonian.
PSD-cone-constrained principal component is a paper-A contribution (k=3 algorithm); paper B has no convex-relaxation counterpart.
Paper A's notion of a desired AMP local optimum (loss <= 6/beta^2) is tied to its iterative algorithm; paper B does not analyze AMP iterates.

Paper A poses Tensor PCA as the optimization problem max <X, v^{otimes k}> s.t. ||v||=1 (the ML estimator). Paper B poses spiked tensor detection AND weak recovery: distinguish WT(d, lambda, X) from WT(d) and recover x. The two problems share input data and have overlapping optima but reflect different framings (optimization vs hypothesis testing / recovery).

Both are the central information-theoretic impossibility result. Paper A's TP402.1 gives a Fano/packing lower bound: beta <= sqrt(k/10) implies E[Loss] >= 1/32. Paper B's TP403.7 is far sharper - a contiguity-based lower bound under conditions (i)-(v) that yields the optimal threshold for each prior. They play the same role (lower bound on detection/recovery) but use fundamentally different machinery (packing+Fano vs second-moment+contiguity), which is exactly what makes B an extension/refinement of A.

All three are the same Auffinger-Ben Arous-Cerny / Crisanti-Sommers / Subag result: the operator (injective) norm of a Gaussian symmetric tensor of order d=k concentrates at mu_d = mu_k. Paper A states it as LP402.1 (with concentration) and TP402.9 (cited limit); paper B states it as TP403.2 (cited). Both attribute it to ABC.

Same explicit Crisanti-Sommers / Auffinger-Ben Arous-Cerny formula characterizing mu_d via the equation (2-d)/d - log(d z^2/2) + (d-1)/2 z^2 - 2/(d^2 z^2) = 0 with z(x) = (x - sqrt(x^2 - 4(d-1)))/((d-1) sqrt(2d)). Identical defining equation in both papers.

Both bound the distinguishability of conditional laws under different spike vectors. Paper A uses a Frobenius-distance KL bound D(P_w || P_w') <= 2(n/k) beta^2; paper B uses the conditioned second-moment formula E_{Q_n}(dP_n / dQ_n)^2 ~ E_{x,x'} exp(n lambda^2 / 2 * beta/(1+beta)) with beta = <x,x'>^d. Different statistics (KL vs chi-squared) but the same role: the central distinguishability quantity feeding into the lower-bound argument.

Paper A's Sudakov-Fernique upper bound on E||X||_op uses a Gaussian-process comparison; paper B's spherical injective-norm bound TP403.9 uses a BBP-eigenvalue argument on a derived spiked matrix instead, so the techniques and statements differ enough to leave LP402.2 unmatched.
Operator-norm bound for unfolded noise M_q(Z) underpins paper A's tensor-unfolding analysis and has no counterpart in paper B.
Technical Gaussian-shift lemma used inside paper A's Sudakov-Fernique proof; not used in paper B.

Paper A's TP402.2 is an ML upper bound for the spherical optimum (Loss <= 2(mu_k + s)/beta when beta >= mu_k). Paper B's analogous upper bounds are: PrP403.2 (cardinality-based MLE for discrete priors) and CP403.1 (spherical strong-detection corollary using L_d(lambda) > mu_d). All three say: above some threshold the ML/MAP/injective-norm estimator detects and approximately recovers the spike; the threshold and proof technique differ across the discrete/spherical settings.
Wedin's perturbation theorem is cited as an external matrix-PCA tool inside paper A's unfolding analysis; paper B does not invoke Wedin.
Tensor-unfolding success threshold (beta >= 5 k^{1/2} n^b) is paper-A-specific; paper B has no algorithmic threshold of this form.
Recursive-unfolding sharp threshold for asymmetric noise is paper-A-specific.
Power-iteration convergence theorem is paper-A-specific.

Both papers derive the same fixed-point equation governing the high-SNR phase but via complementary heuristics. Paper A obtains, rigorously via AMP state evolution (PrP402.1, TP402.7), the recursion tau_{t+1}^2 = beta^2 (tau_t^2/(1+tau_t^2))^{k-1} and its fixed-point equation 1/beta^2 = x^{k-2}(1-x). Paper B obtains, via the replica method (EP403.4 Rademacher, EP403.5 spherical), the saddle equations lambda^2/2 * d * q^{d-1} (1-q) = q (spherical) and a Tap-style Rademacher equation. Both predict (lambda^*)^2 ~ 2 log d for the spherical prior at large d; RP403.4 makes this explicit. The relation is conjectured-equivalent: AMP state evolution and replica saddle agree on the spiked tensor model.
Tensor unfolding (matrix PCA on M_q(X)) is a paper-A algorithmic contribution; paper B does not analyze polynomial-time spectral algorithms.
Recursive unfolding is paper-A-specific.
Tensor power iteration is paper-A-specific; paper B's algorithms (AP403.1-3) are MLE/MAP/injective-norm exhaustive maximizers, not iterative.
Warm-start power iteration is paper-A-specific.
AMP for tensor PCA is paper-A-specific.
PSD-cone-constrained projected power iteration is paper-A-specific.

Paper B's MLE detector for discrete priors thresholds an exhaustive search over supp(X), exploiting the cardinality bound. Paper A does not consider exhaustive-search detection over discrete priors and has no counterpart.
MAP detector with entropy correction is paper-B-specific.

Injective-norm detector for the spherical prior thresholds ||T|| at a level between mu_d and L_d(lambda); paper A's ML estimator (ProbP402.1) is closely related but is presented as an optimization problem rather than a thresholded hypothesis test. The conceptual overlap is captured by the ProbP402.1 / ProbP403.1 match above; AP403.3 itself has no algorithmic counterpart in A.

Both prove the central impossibility theorem (TP402.1 vs TP403.7). Paper A's PP402.1 is a packing + Fano + KL-bound argument. Paper B's PP403.8 is a noise-conditioned second-moment / chi-squared argument that gives the exact threshold. Same theorem role, fundamentally different proof technique - this is what makes B's analysis a refinement of A's.

Composite L2 alignment of the two proof-step DAGs of the central lower bound. Paper A's four steps - pack the sphere, Markov, Fano with KL, choose epsilon - implement the packing strategy. Paper B's eight steps - define noise-conditioned distribution, reduce chi^2 to m(x,x'), split |beta| in/out of [eps,1], bound M_1 via rate function, bound M_2 via local subgaussianity, conclude contiguity/TV/non-recovery - implement the second-moment strategy. The DAGs are not step-by-step alignable; this composite entry encodes that both decompose into a setup-bound-conclude pipeline but with different machinery.
Proof of LP402.3 (operator norm of unfolded noise) is paper-A-specific.
Proof of Wedin's perturbation theorem is paper-A-specific (and externally cited).
Proof of the unfolding success threshold is paper-A-specific.
Proof of recursive-unfolding result is paper-A-specific.
Proof of power-iteration convergence is paper-A-specific.
Proof of AMP convergence threshold is paper-A-specific.

Proof of ML upper bound (TP402.2) uses Gaussian isoperimetry on Lipschitz functionals; paper B's spherical upper bound CP403.1 has a distinct BBP-eigenvalue proof (PP403.4) that handles a related but technically different statement, captured in the TP402.2 / CP403.1 match above.
Proof of LP402.2 (Sudakov-Fernique upper bound) is paper-A-specific.
Proof of KL bound between conditional laws is paper-A-specific.
Spherical prior X_sph as a formal prior on unit vectors is paper-B-specific (paper A treats the spike as a fixed unit vector v_z).
Rademacher prior X_Rade is paper-B-specific.
Sparse Rademacher prior is paper-B-specific.
Strong / weak detection and weak recovery definitions are paper-B-specific framing of the inference problem.
Rate function f_X is the central technical object of paper B's lower-bound machinery; no counterpart in paper A.
Locally subgaussian prior is part of paper B's hypothesis (iv) for the main lower bound; no counterpart in paper A.
Sparse Rademacher rate function f_rho is paper-B-specific.
Spherical prior large-d threshold (sqrt(2 log d)) is a paper-B contribution combining the lower bound TP403.8 and upper bound CP403.1.
Rademacher prior large-d threshold is paper-B-specific.
Sparse Rademacher prior large-d threshold is paper-B-specific.
Sparse Rademacher rho -> 0 asymptotics is paper-B-specific.
Spherical prior lower bound (specialization of TP403.7) is paper-B-specific.

Spherical-prior injective-norm lower bound L_d(lambda) is paper-B's tightening of the upper bound below mu_d via a BBP eigenvalue argument; paper A's looser ML upper bound TP402.2 uses Gaussian isoperimetry instead.
Rademacher-prior lower bound is paper-B-specific.
Sparse Rademacher lower bound for each d is paper-B-specific.
Chernoff implication lemma (technical reduction inside the lower-bound theorem) is paper-B-specific.
MAP entropy-based upper bound is paper-B-specific.
Renyi/collision-entropy lower bound at large d is paper-B-specific.
Sparse Rademacher tail-bound machinery is paper-B-specific.
Spherical rate function lemma is paper-B-specific.
Paper B's open problems (matrix-case non-recovery from chi^2 and supercritical energy landscape) are paper-B-specific. Paper A has no open_problem nodes.
